Chapter 1 topics

Ch 1 Structural Organisation in Animals — Animal Tissues

In multicellular animals, cells rarely act alone. Groups of similar cells that perform a common function are organised together into a tissue. Different tissues combine to form organs, organs combine into organ systems, and organ systems together make up the complete organism. Animal tissues are broadly grouped into four fundamental types: Epithelial, Connective, Muscular and Neural.

1. Levels of Structural Organisation

Figure Z1.1: Hierarchy of structural organisation — from a single cell to the complete organism.

The study of tissues is called Histology. Based on origin and function, all animal tissues fall into four fundamental categories, summarised below and detailed in the sections that follow.

Tissue TypePrimary Function
EpithelialCovering & lining of body surfaces, secretion, protection
ConnectiveBinds, supports and connects other tissues/organs
MuscularProduces movement through contraction
NeuralReceives & transmits stimuli; coordination

2. Epithelial Tissue

Epithelial tissue covers the body surface and lines body cavities, ducts and internal organs. Cells are tightly packed with very little intercellular matrix, sit on a basement membrane, and are avascular (get nourishment by diffusion). Classified by cell shape and number of layers:

Figure Z1.2: Major types of epithelial cells classified by shape — squamous, cuboidal, columnar, ciliated columnar and glandular.
Simple Epithelium: Single layer of cells; found where absorption/filtration/secretion occurs — e.g. lining of blood vessels, kidney tubules, gut lining.
Compound Epithelium: Multiple cell layers; provides protection with little role in secretion/absorption — e.g. skin, oesophagus lining.
Glandular Epithelium: Modified for secretion. Exocrine glands (sweat, salivary) secrete via ducts; endocrine glands (thyroid, pituitary) are ductless, secreting hormones directly into blood.
Special Junctions: Epithelial cells are held together by tight junctions (prevent leakage), adhering junctions (mechanical strength) and gap junctions (allow cell-to-cell communication).

3. Connective Tissue

The most abundant and widely distributed tissue — it links, supports and binds other tissues. Unlike epithelium, connective tissue cells are sparsely arranged and embedded in an abundant intercellular matrix, which may be jelly-like, fluid, dense or rigid.

CategoryExamplesKey Feature
Connective tissue proper (loose)Areolar tissue, Adipose tissueFills space inside organs, fat storage
Connective tissue proper (dense)Tendons, LigamentsTendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone — both very strong, poorly vascular
Skeletal (supportive)Cartilage, BoneCartilage: smooth, solid matrix (chondrocytes); Bone: hard, calcified matrix (osteocytes)
Fluid connective tissueBloodPlasma matrix carrying RBCs, WBCs & platelets; transports gases, nutrients, wastes
Figure Z1.3: Representative connective tissues — loose areolar tissue, cartilage (chondrocytes in lacunae), and fluid connective tissue (blood).

4. Muscular Tissue

Made of elongated cells called muscle fibres, containing contractile proteins (actin & myosin) that enable movement.

Figure Z1.4: The three types of muscle tissue — skeletal (striated, voluntary), smooth (unstriated, involuntary) and cardiac (branched, involuntary, with intercalated discs).
TypeLocationControlNucleus
SkeletalAttached to bonesVoluntaryMultinucleate, peripheral
SmoothGut wall, blood vessels, irisInvoluntarySingle, central
CardiacHeart wallInvoluntarySingle, central; joined by intercalated discs

5. Neural Tissue

Made up of highly specialised cells called neurons, designed to receive, conduct and transmit electrical impulses for coordination of body activities. Supporting neuroglial cells protect and nourish neurons.

Figure Z1.5: Structure of a typical neuron — dendrites receive impulses, the cyton (cell body) integrates them, and the myelinated axon conducts the impulse to axon terminals for transmission to the next cell.
Impulse flow: Dendrite → Cell body (Cyton) → Axon → Axon terminal → Synapse → next neuron/effector organ.
Chapter 2 topics

Ch 2 Biomolecules

Every living cell is a self-contained chemical factory. If you analyse the chemical composition of a cell, you will find both inorganic constituents (water, mineral ions, gases) and organic constituents — the true biomolecules: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. This chapter looks at the structure, classification and biological role of each class, and how small building-block molecules polymerise into the giant macromolecules of life.

1. Chemical Composition of the Cell

If you take a tissue, grind it in trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and filter it, you get an acid-soluble pool (small molecules — amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, etc.) and a filter residue made of larger macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids). Elemental analysis shows carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen make up the bulk of dry weight, with smaller amounts of phosphorus, sulphur and trace elements.

Figure Z2.1: Separating a cell's chemical constituents into the acid-soluble pool of micromolecules and the macromolecule-rich filter residue.
Biomolecule ClassBuilding Block (Monomer)Bond Linking Monomers
Carbohydrates (polysaccharides)MonosaccharidesGlycosidic bond
ProteinsAmino acidsPeptide bond
Nucleic AcidsNucleotidesPhosphodiester bond
LipidsGlycerol + fatty acidsEster bond
NEET point: Water is the most abundant chemical in any living tissue (60–90%), acting as an excellent solvent and medium for metabolic reactions.

2. Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, the chief source of energy and important structural components. Based on the number of sugar units, they are classified into three groups:

Figure Z2.2: Classification of carbohydrates by chain length — monosaccharides join via glycosidic bonds to form oligosaccharides and, ultimately, long-chain polysaccharides.

A glycosidic bond forms between two monosaccharides by loss of a water molecule (condensation/dehydration reaction) — e.g. glucose + glucose → maltose. Polysaccharides can be homopolysaccharides (one type of monomer, e.g. starch, cellulose — both made only of glucose) or heteropolysaccharides (more than one type of monomer).

PolysaccharideFound InFunction
StarchPlants (amylose + amylopectin)Storage form of glucose
GlycogenAnimals, fungi (liver, muscle)Storage form of glucose in animals
CellulosePlant cell wallsStructural — unbranched glucose chain
ChitinInsect exoskeleton, fungal cell wallStructural polysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine
NEET point: Starch gives a blue-black colour with iodine; it's a branched (amylopectin) + unbranched (amylose) glucose polymer, unlike cellulose which is a straight, unbranched chain.

3. Proteins

Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Every amino acid has a central (α) carbon bonded to an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom, and a variable side chain (R group) that gives each of the 20 amino acids its distinct identity.

Figure Z2.3: General structure of an amino acid, and formation of a peptide bond between two amino acids by loss of a water molecule (dehydration/condensation).

Amino acids are grouped as essential (cannot be synthesised by the body, must come from diet, e.g. valine, leucine) and non-essential (body can synthesise them, e.g. glycine, alanine). A chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds is a polypeptide; a functional protein may consist of one or more polypeptide chains folded into a specific 3-D shape.

Figure Z2.4: Four levels of protein structure — from the linear amino acid sequence (primary) to multi-subunit assemblies (quaternary), e.g. haemoglobin's four polypeptide chains.
NEET point: Collagen (most abundant protein in animals) and trypsin are common NEET examples. Haemoglobin shows quaternary structure with 2 α- and 2 β-globin chains.

4. Lipids

Lipids are generally water-insoluble (hydrophobic), often containing fatty acids. A fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group that can be a methyl (–CH₃), ethyl, or a longer hydrocarbon chain. If the hydrocarbon chain has no double bonds, it is a saturated fatty acid; with one or more double bonds, it is unsaturated.

Figure Z2.5: A triglyceride is formed by esterification of glycerol with three fatty acid molecules.
Lipid TypeCompositionExample / Role
Simple lipids (fats/oils)Glycerol + fatty acidsEnergy storage (adipose tissue)
PhospholipidsGlycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate groupMajor component of cell membranes (e.g. lecithin)
SteroidsFused ring structure, no fatty acidsCholesterol, sex hormones
WaxesLong chain fatty acid + long chain alcoholWaterproof coatings (skin, cuticle)
NEET point: Ghee/butter are saturated fats (solid at room temperature); groundnut/til oil are unsaturated fats (liquid at room temperature).

5. Nucleic Acids

Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three components: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. A base + sugar alone (without phosphate) is called a nucleoside.

Figure Z2.6: Structure of a single nucleotide, and how successive nucleotides link via phosphodiester bonds to build a polynucleotide chain.

Nitrogenous bases are of two types: purines (double-ring — Adenine, Guanine) and pyrimidines (single-ring — Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil). In the DNA double helix, bases pair specifically: A = T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G ≡ C (3 hydrogen bonds) — this is complementary base pairing. The two polynucleotide strands run antiparallel to each other, as established by Watson and Crick (1953).

FeatureDNARNA
SugarDeoxyriboseRibose
Pyrimidine baseThymine (T)Uracil (U) instead of Thymine
StrandsDouble-stranded helixUsually single-stranded
FunctionStores genetic informationmRNA, tRNA, rRNA — protein synthesis
NEET point: Adenine always pairs with Thymine (or Uracil in RNA); Guanine always pairs with Cytosine — remember "Purine pairs with Pyrimidine" to keep helix width constant.

6. Enzymes

Enzymes are (mostly) proteins that act as biocatalysts — they speed up biochemical reactions without being consumed, by lowering the activation energy. Each enzyme has a specific 3-D pocket called the active site where the substrate binds.

Figure Z2.7: Enzyme action (induced fit model) — the substrate binds the active site, forms an enzyme-substrate complex, reaction occurs, and the unchanged enzyme is released along with the product.

Enzyme activity is affected by temperature and pH — each enzyme has an optimum temperature/pH range for maximum activity, beyond which the protein denatures and activity falls. Enzymes are classified into six major classes based on the reaction they catalyse:

ClassType of Reaction Catalysed
OxidoreductasesOxidation-reduction between two substrates
TransferasesTransfer of a group between substrates
HydrolasesHydrolysis (transfer of group to water)
LyasesRemoval of a group to form a double bond
IsomerasesRearrangement within a molecule (isomer formation)
LigasesJoining two molecules using ATP energy
Chapter 3 topics

Ch 3 Breathing and Exchange of Gases

Every living cell needs a continuous supply of O₂ to oxidise food and release energy, and must get rid of the CO₂ produced. Breathing (respiration in the physical sense) is the mechanical process of taking in atmospheric air rich in O₂ and giving out CO₂-rich alveolar air. The energy-releasing biochemical process inside cells is cellular respiration — a separate topic. This chapter covers respiratory organs, the human respiratory system, breathing mechanics, gas exchange/transport, and their regulation.

1. Respiratory Organs Across the Animal Kingdom

Different animal groups use different respiratory structures depending on habitat and complexity:

Animal GroupRespiratory Organ
Lower invertebrates (Protozoans, sponges, coelenterates)General body surface (diffusion)
Earthworm (Annelids)Moist cuticle (skin)
InsectsTracheal tubes (network opening via spiracles)
Fish, PrawnsGills
AmphibiansMoist skin + Lungs (dual respiration)
Reptiles, Birds, MammalsLungs
NEET point: In insects, tracheal tubes carry O₂ directly to tissues — the blood (haemolymph) plays no role in O₂ transport in insects, unlike in vertebrates.

2. Human Respiratory System

Air enters through the external nares (nostrils) → nasal chamber (lined with mucus + hair to filter dust and warm/moisten air) → pharynx → larynx (voice box, contains vocal cords) → trachea (windpipe, supported by C-shaped cartilage rings that prevent collapse) → primary bronchi (one to each lung) → bronchioles → alveoli (site of gas exchange).

Figure Z3.1: Human respiratory pathway — nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → lungs (bronchioles and alveoli).

Each lung is covered by a double-layered membrane, the pleura — the outer parietal pleura (attached to the thoracic wall) and the inner visceral pleura (attached to the lung surface), with pleural fluid between them reducing friction.

3. Mechanism of Breathing

Breathing involves two stages — inspiration (air moves in) and expiration (air moves out) — driven by pressure/volume changes in the thoracic cavity, following Boyle's Law (pressure is inversely proportional to volume).

Figure Z3.2: During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and the ribs move outward, increasing thoracic volume and drawing air in; expiration reverses these changes, pushing air out.

Inspiration is normally active (needs muscle contraction — diaphragm + external intercostal muscles); quiet expiration is largely passive (elastic recoil of lungs and relaxation of muscles), though forced expiration involves internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.

4. Respiratory Volumes and Capacities

A spirometer measures the volume of air a person inhales/exhales, helping assess pulmonary function. Approximate values for a healthy human adult:

TermDefinitionApprox. Value
Tidal Volume (TV)Air breathed in/out in normal (quiet) respiration~500 mL
Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV)Extra air inhaled by forcible inspiration beyond TV~2500–3000 mL
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV)Extra air exhaled by forcible expiration beyond TV~1000–1100 mL
Residual Volume (RV)Air remaining in lungs even after forcible expiration~1100–1200 mL
Vital Capacity (VC = TV+IRV+ERV)Maximum air a person can breathe out after forced inspiration~3700–4600 mL
Total Lung Capacity (TLC = VC+RV)Total air volume the lungs can hold~4500–6000 mL
NEET point: A person breathes in/out ~6000–8000 mL of air per minute at rest (12–16 breaths × 500 mL tidal volume).

5. Exchange and Transport of Gases

Gas exchange happens by simple diffusion, driven by the partial pressure gradient (pO₂ and pCO₂) between alveoli, blood and tissues — across a very thin alveolar-capillary membrane.

Figure Z3.3: O₂ diffuses down its pressure gradient from alveoli → blood → tissues, while CO₂ diffuses the opposite way, from tissues → blood → alveoli.

O₂ transport: ~97% is carried by haemoglobin (Hb) as oxyhaemoglobin (4 O₂ per Hb molecule); only ~3% dissolves directly in plasma. Binding of O₂ to Hb is influenced by pO₂, pCO₂, H⁺ concentration and temperature — high pCO₂, low pH and high temperature (as in active tissues) favour O₂ unloading (Bohr effect).

CO₂ transport: ~70% as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻, via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs), ~20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin (bound to Hb), and only ~7% dissolved in plasma.

6. Regulation of Respiration & Disorders

Breathing is regulated by the nervous system to keep pace with the body's demands. The main respiratory rhythm centre is in the medulla oblongata, which continuously generates the rhythm of inspiration/expiration. The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the medulla's rhythm and reduce inspiration duration. A chemosensitive area adjacent to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺ ions — a rise in these strongly stimulates the centre for corrective action, making CO₂ (not O₂) the primary respiratory stimulus.

DisorderDescription
AsthmaDifficulty in breathing due to inflammation/spasm of bronchi and bronchioles
EmphysemaChronic disorder — alveolar walls damaged (often by smoking), reducing surface area for gas exchange
Occupational respiratory disordersCaused by long-term exposure to dust (e.g. silicosis in stone/mining workers) causing fibrosis
NEET point: The chemosensitive area is far more sensitive to CO₂/H⁺ than O₂ — this is why CO₂ level, not O₂ level, is the main driver of respiratory rate.
Chapter 4 topics

Ch 4 Body Fluids and Circulation

Multicellular animals need an efficient transport system to carry O₂, nutrients, hormones, wastes and heat to and from every cell. In humans this job is done by two body fluids — blood and lymph — driven around the body by the heart. This chapter covers blood composition, blood groups, clotting, lymph, heart structure, the cardiac cycle and double circulation.

1. Composition of Blood

Blood is a special connective tissue with a fluid matrix (plasma) and formed elements (cells) suspended in it.

Figure Z4.1: Blood composition — a fluid plasma matrix carrying proteins/ions/nutrients, plus formed cellular elements (RBCs, WBCs, platelets).
Formed ElementKey FeatureFunction
RBC (Erythrocytes)Most abundant; biconcave, anucleate in mammals; contain haemoglobinO₂ / CO₂ transport
WBC (Leucocytes)Nucleated; 5 types — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, lymphocytesImmunity / defence
Platelets (Thrombocytes)Cell fragments from megakaryocytesBlood clotting
NEET point: Among WBCs, neutrophils are most abundant (~60–65%) and basophils least abundant (~0.5–1%). Remember the mnemonic "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas" for Neutrophil–Lymphocyte–Monocyte–Eosinophil–Basophil (decreasing abundance).

2. Blood Groups and Blood Clotting

The ABO blood group system is based on the presence/absence of surface antigens (A, B) on RBCs, and corresponding antibodies in plasma:

Blood GroupAntigen on RBCAntibody in Plasma
AAAnti-B
BBAnti-A
ABA and BNone — universal recipient
ONone — universal donorAnti-A and Anti-B

The Rh factor is another RBC antigen; Rh⁺ individuals have it, Rh⁻ individuals don't. Rh incompatibility between an Rh⁻ mother and Rh⁺ foetus can cause erythroblastosis foetalis in a subsequent Rh⁺ pregnancy.

Figure Z4.2: Simplified blood clotting cascade — thromboplastin release activates the prothrombin–thrombin–fibrinogen–fibrin sequence, forming a clot mesh.

3. Lymph (Tissue Fluid)

As blood passes through capillaries, some plasma (minus large proteins) filters out into intercellular spaces, forming interstitial/tissue fluid. This fluid is drained into the lymphatic system as lymph — a colourless fluid containing less protein than plasma and rich in lymphocytes.

Functions of lymph: returns tissue fluid/proteins to the blood, transports absorbed fats from the intestine (via lacteals), and plays a key role in the body's immune/defence mechanism.

4. Human Heart — Structure

The human heart is myogenic (initiates its own beat) and has four chambers — two upper thin-walled atria and two lower thick-walled ventricles, separated by the interatrial and interventricular septa.

Figure Z4.3: Four-chambered human heart — right side (deoxygenated blood) separated from left side (oxygenated blood) by septa; tricuspid and bicuspid valves prevent backflow between atria and ventricles.

The heart has a specialised conduction system: the Sino-Atrial Node (SAN) in the right atrium (the "pacemaker", generating the highest rate of impulses), the Atrio-Ventricular Node (AVN), the AV bundle (Bundle of His), and Purkinje fibres that spread the impulse through the ventricles.

5. Cardiac Cycle and ECG

One complete heartbeat — atrial systole, ventricular systole, and joint diastole — is a cardiac cycle, lasting about 0.8 seconds (~72 beats/minute at rest). Each cycle produces two heart sounds: "lub" (closure of tricuspid/bicuspid valves) and "dub" (closure of semilunar valves).

Figure Z4.4: A normal ECG trace showing the P wave, QRS complex, and T wave that correspond to the electrical events of one cardiac cycle.
NEET point: Cardiac output = Stroke volume × Heart rate. With a stroke volume of ~70 mL and heart rate of ~72/min, cardiac output ≈ 5000 mL (5 L) per minute.

6. Double Circulation and Regulation

Human blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit — double circulation — made up of two circuits:

Figure Z4.5: Double circulation — the pulmonary circuit (heart ↔ lungs, for oxygenation) and the systemic circuit (heart ↔ body tissues, for delivering oxygenated blood), both passing through the heart.

Cardiac activity is myogenic (initiated by the SAN itself) but is modulated by a neural centre in the medulla oblongata, which can increase heart rate via sympathetic nerves or decrease it via the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve. Adrenal medullary hormones (adrenaline, noradrenaline) can also increase cardiac output.

NEET point: Hypertension (persistently high BP, ≥140/90 mmHg) and Coronary Artery Disease (blockage of coronary arteries by fat/cholesterol deposits, causing angina/heart attack) are key circulatory disorders to remember.

Chapter 1 topics

Ch 1 Units and Dimensions

Physics is a science of measurement. Every measurable property — length, mass, time, temperature — is a physical quantity, and every measurement is meaningless without a standard reference called a unit. This chapter builds the toolkit used throughout physics: standard units, dimensional formulae, and rules for handling measured numbers.

1. Physical Quantities — Fundamental & Derived

A quantity that can be measured and expressed in terms of a numerical value and a unit is a physical quantity. These are divided into two kinds:

Fundamental (Base) Quantities: Independent quantities not defined in terms of any other quantity — e.g. length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, luminous intensity, amount of substance.
Derived Quantities: Obtained by combining fundamental quantities — e.g. speed (length/time), force (mass × length/time²), area, volume, density.

2. The SI System — Seven Base Units

The International System of Units (SI) is the globally accepted system, built from seven independent base units:

Physical QuantitySI UnitSymbol
Lengthmetrem
Masskilogramkg
Timeseconds
Electric CurrentampereA
Thermodynamic TemperaturekelvinK
Amount of Substancemolemol
Luminous Intensitycandelacd
Supplementary Units: Radian (rad) for plane angle and Steradian (sr) for solid angle — dimensionless quantities used alongside the seven base units.

3. Dimensions & Dimensional Formula

The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers to which the base quantities are raised to represent it. The seven base dimensions are written as [M] mass, [L] length, [T] time, [A] current, [K] temperature, [mol] amount, [cd] luminous intensity.

Figure P1.1: Deriving a dimensional formula by expressing a derived quantity in terms of base quantities.
QuantityFormulaDimensional Formula
AreaLength × Breadth[M⁰L²T⁰]
VelocityDisplacement / Time[M⁰L¹T⁻¹]
AccelerationVelocity / Time[M⁰L¹T⁻²]
ForceMass × Acceleration[M¹L¹T⁻²]
Work / EnergyForce × Distance[M¹L²T⁻²]
PowerWork / Time[M¹L²T⁻³]
PressureForce / Area[M¹L⁻¹T⁻²]
DensityMass / Volume[M¹L⁻³T⁰]

4. Dimensional Analysis — Principle of Homogeneity

The Principle of Homogeneity states that the dimensions of every term on both sides of a correct physical equation must be identical. This gives dimensional analysis three major uses:

1. Checking correctness: Verify an equation by confirming both sides have the same dimensional formula.
2. Deriving relationships: Find how a quantity depends on others, when the form of dependence is unknown (e.g. deriving the time period of a simple pendulum, T ∝ √(l/g)).
3. Converting units: Convert a physical quantity from one system of units to another.
Limitations: Cannot determine dimensionless constants; fails for equations involving trigonometric, exponential or logarithmic functions; cannot be used if a quantity depends on more than 3 unknown factors.

5. Significant Figures

Significant figures in a measured value are all the digits that are reliably known, plus one estimated (uncertain) digit — they indicate the precision of a measurement.

Rules for Counting Significant Figures:
  • All non-zero digits are significant (e.g. 1234 → 4 sig. figs).
  • Zeros between two non-zero digits are significant (e.g. 1002 → 4 sig. figs).
  • Leading zeros (before the first non-zero digit) are NOT significant (e.g. 0.0025 → 2 sig. figs).
  • Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (e.g. 2.500 → 4 sig. figs).
  • Trailing zeros in a number without a decimal point are ambiguous unless written in scientific notation (2500 → best written as 2.5 × 10³ for 2 sig. figs).

6. Errors in Measurement

No physical measurement is ever perfectly exact — the difference between the measured value and the true value is called error.

Type of ErrorDescription
Systematic ErrorConsistent, one-directional error from a known cause (instrumental, personal, or environmental) — can be minimised by correcting the method.
Random ErrorIrregular, unpredictable fluctuations with no fixed cause — reduced by taking multiple readings and averaging.
Gross ErrorLarge error due to carelessness of the observer, e.g. misreading a scale.
Measure of ErrorFormula
Absolute ErrorΔaᵢ = |aₘₑₐₙ − aᵢ|
Mean Absolute ErrorΔa = (Σ|Δaᵢ|) / n
Relative ErrorΔa / aₘₑₐₙ
Percentage Error(Δa / aₘₑₐₙ) × 100
Combination of Errors
  • Addition/Subtraction: absolute errors add up — Δ(a ± b) = Δa + Δb
  • Multiplication/Division: relative errors add up — Δz/z = Δa/a + Δb/b
  • Power relation (z = aⁿ): Δz/z = n × (Δa/a)

7. Vernier Caliper

The Vernier Caliper is a precision instrument used to measure lengths, diameters (internal & external) and depths to an accuracy far greater than an ordinary metre scale, by using an auxiliary sliding scale — the vernier scale — alongside a fixed main scale.

Figure P1.2: Parts of a Vernier Caliper — main scale (fixed), sliding vernier scale, external jaws (outer diameter), internal jaws (not shown, on the reverse side, for inner diameter), and depth rod (for depth of a hole/cavity).
Main Scale: A rigid steel scale graduated in cm/mm, fixed to the body of the instrument. It gives the reading up to the last full main-scale division before the vernier's zero.
Vernier Scale: A smaller sliding scale with divisions slightly smaller than the main scale's, used to measure the fractional part of a main scale division very precisely.

Least Count of a Vernier Caliper

Least Count (LC) = 1 Main Scale Division (MSD) − 1 Vernier Scale Division (VSD)

Standard Example: If 1 MSD = 1 mm, and 10 VSD = 9 MSD (i.e. 1 VSD = 0.9 mm),
LC = 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm (the most common vernier caliper least count).

Taking a Reading

Total Reading = Main Scale Reading (MSR) + (Vernier Coincidence Number × Least Count) ± Zero Error

where the Vernier Coincidence Number is the vernier division that exactly coincides with any main scale division.

Zero Error

When the jaws are fully closed, the vernier zero should coincide exactly with the main scale zero. Any deviation is the zero error, which must be subtracted from every raw reading:

  • Positive Zero Error: Vernier zero lies to the right of main scale zero → subtract the error from the observed reading. (Instrument reads a value larger than the true value.)
  • Negative Zero Error: Vernier zero lies to the left of main scale zero → add the (numerically negative) error, i.e. add its magnitude to the observed reading.

Correct/True Reading = Observed Reading − Zero Error

Common uses: External jaws — outer diameter/length of an object; Internal jaws — internal diameter of a hollow tube/ring; Depth rod — depth of a hole, groove or beaker.

8. Screw Gauge (Micrometer Screw Gauge)

The Screw Gauge is used to measure very small dimensions — such as the diameter of a thin wire, thickness of a sheet of paper, or a small ball bearing — with even greater precision than a vernier caliper, typically down to 0.01 mm or 0.001 mm. It works on the principle of a screw thread: one complete rotation of the screw advances it by a fixed, known distance.

Figure P1.3: Parts of a Screw Gauge — U-frame with anvil (fixed) and spindle (moving), sleeve carrying the main (linear) scale, rotating thimble carrying the circular scale, and the ratchet that prevents over-tightening.
Anvil & Spindle: The object to be measured is placed between the fixed anvil and the moving spindle tip.
Sleeve (Main Scale): A linear mm-scale engraved on the fixed sleeve, read against the edge of the thimble.
Thimble (Circular Scale): Rotates with the spindle; usually has 50 or 100 divisions around its circumference.
Ratchet: Slips with a click sound once a fixed, safe pressure is applied — prevents damage to the object or thread from over-tightening.

Pitch & Least Count

Pitch = Distance moved by spindle on main scale / Number of full rotations of the thimble

Least Count (LC) = Pitch / Total number of divisions on the circular (thimble) scale

Standard Example: If Pitch = 1 mm and the circular scale has 100 divisions,
LC = 1 mm / 100 = 0.01 mm — ten times finer than a typical vernier caliper.

Taking a Reading

Total Reading = Main Scale (Pitch Scale) Reading + (Circular Scale Reading × Least Count) ± Zero Error

Zero Error in a Screw Gauge

When the anvil and spindle are brought together (nothing in between), the zero of the circular scale should align exactly with the reference line on the main scale.

  • Positive Zero Error: Circular scale's zero is below the reference line → instrument over-reads → subtract the error.
  • Negative Zero Error: Circular scale's zero is above the reference line → instrument under-reads → add the magnitude of the error.

Correct/True Reading = Observed Reading − Zero Error

Sources of Error to Avoid
  • Backlash Error: Occurs if the screw's direction of rotation is reversed mid-measurement — the spindle may not move immediately due to worn threads. Avoided by always rotating the screw in the same direction while approaching the object.
  • Always use the ratchet (not the thimble directly) to close the gap on the object, to apply uniform, safe pressure.
  • Take the mean of several readings, and check for zero error before and after the measurement.
Chapter 2 topics

Ch 2 Vectors

Physical quantities like distance and speed need only a number and unit to be fully described — these are scalars. But quantities like displacement, velocity and force also need a direction — these are vectors. This chapter covers vector representation, types, addition/subtraction, and the two ways of "multiplying" vectors — the dot and cross products.

1. Scalars and Vectors

A scalar quantity has only magnitude (e.g. mass, distance, speed, temperature, work, energy). A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction, and obeys the laws of vector addition (e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum). A vector is represented by an arrow: the length shows magnitude, the arrowhead shows direction.

Figure P2.1: A vector drawn as an arrow — length represents magnitude, arrowhead shows direction; θ is the angle the vector makes with a reference axis.

2. Types of Vectors

TypeDefinition
Unit Vector (Â)Magnitude 1, gives only direction: Â = A⃗ / |A⃗|. Standard unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x, y, z axes
Zero (Null) VectorMagnitude zero, direction undefined (e.g. A⃗ + (−A⃗) = 0⃗)
Equal VectorsSame magnitude and same direction (position doesn't matter)
Negative VectorSame magnitude, opposite direction to the given vector
Collinear VectorsLie along the same line or parallel lines
Coplanar VectorsLie in the same plane
Position VectorSpecifies the position of a point with respect to origin
NEET point: A unit vector only tells direction, never magnitude — it is dimensionless and always has magnitude exactly 1.

3. Resolution of Vectors into Components

Any vector A⃗ in a plane can be broken (resolved) into two mutually perpendicular components along the x and y axes:

Figure P2.2: Resolving vector A⃗ into perpendicular components Aₓ = A cos θ and Aᵧ = A sin θ, so that A⃗ = Aₓ î + Aᵧ ĵ.

Magnitude: |A⃗| = √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ²)  |  Direction: tan θ = Aᵧ / Aₓ

4. Addition of Vectors

Vectors add geometrically (not arithmetically) since direction matters. Two common laws:

Figure P2.3: Triangle Law — place B⃗'s tail at A⃗'s head, resultant R⃗ joins A⃗'s tail to B⃗'s head. Parallelogram Law — vectors from a common point form adjacent sides; resultant is the diagonal.

|R⃗| = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)  |  tan α = (B sin θ) / (A + B cos θ)

NEET point: Maximum resultant occurs when θ = 0° (Rmax = A+B); minimum when θ = 180° (Rmin = |A−B|). Vector addition is commutative (A⃗+B⃗ = B⃗+A⃗) and associative.

5. Subtraction of Vectors

Subtracting B⃗ from A⃗ is the same as adding A⃗ and the negative of B⃗: A⃗ − B⃗ = A⃗ + (−B⃗). Reverse the direction of B⃗ and apply the triangle/parallelogram law.

Figure P2.4: Vector subtraction A⃗ − B⃗ is performed by reversing B⃗'s direction and adding it to A⃗ using the triangle law.

6. Dot Product (Scalar Product)

The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar result: A⃗ · B⃗ = AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between them. Geometrically, it is the product of one vector's magnitude and the projection of the other onto it. Example: Work done, W = F⃗ · d⃗.

Figure P2.5: The dot product equals |B⃗| multiplied by the projection of A⃗ along B⃗ (i.e. A cos θ) — the result is a pure scalar (no direction).
CaseAngle θResult
Parallel vectors0°A⃗ · B⃗ = AB (maximum)
Perpendicular vectors90°A⃗ · B⃗ = 0
Anti-parallel vectors180°A⃗ · B⃗ = −AB (minimum)

î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1  |  î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0

7. Cross Product (Vector Product)

The cross product of two vectors gives a vector result: A⃗ × B⃗ = AB sin θ n̂, where n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane containing A⃗ and B⃗, and its direction is found using the right-hand rule. Example: Torque, τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗.

Figure P2.6: The cross product A⃗ × B⃗ is a vector perpendicular to both A⃗ and B⃗, with direction given by the right-hand rule; its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by A⃗ and B⃗.
CaseAngle θResult
Parallel vectors0°A⃗ × B⃗ = 0⃗ (minimum)
Perpendicular vectors90°|A⃗ × B⃗| = AB (maximum)

î×ĵ = k̂,  ĵ×k̂ = î,  k̂×î = ĵ  |  A⃗ × B⃗ = −(B⃗ × A⃗) (anti-commutative)

NEET point: Cross product is NOT commutative — order matters and reversing it flips the sign. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.

Chapter 1: Cell — The Unit of Life (Class 11 NEET Foundation)

Every living thing you can name — a banyan tree, a blue whale, or a single bacterium floating in a pond — is built from the same basic unit: the cell. It is the smallest structure capable of carrying out all the functions of life independently: it can take in nutrients, convert them into energy, grow, respond to its surroundings, and reproduce. This idea took nearly two centuries of careful microscopy and debate to become a formal theory.

Figure 1.1: Timeline of key discoveries leading to the modern Cell Theory

Robert Hooke (1665)

Using a self-built compound microscope, Hooke examined a thin slice of cork and observed row upon row of small, empty box-like compartments. He named them "cellulae" (Latin for small rooms). What he actually saw were the dead cell walls of cork tissue — not living cells — since cork is non-living plant tissue.

Anton von Leeuwenhoek (1674)

Using hand-ground lenses of very high quality, Leeuwenhoek was the first person to see and describe a living cell. He observed free-living cells in pond water — bacteria, protozoa (which he called "animalcules"), and even blood cells and sperm cells.

Robert Brown (1831)

A Scottish botanist who, while studying orchid cells under the microscope, discovered a dense, roughly spherical structure inside every cell and named it the nucleus. This was the first organelle to be described.

Purkinje (1839)

Introduced the term "protoplasm" for the fluid substance of the cell, later understood to be the living material — the physical basis of life — within which the nucleus and organelles are suspended.

The Cell Theory — Formal Statement
  • M. Schleiden (1838): German botanist; examined many plant tissues and concluded that all plants are composed of cells.
  • T. Schwann (1839): British zoologist; extended the idea to animal tissues, discovered the plasma membrane, and noted that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together, Schleiden and Schwann formulated the Cell Theory: all living organisms are composed of cells and cells are the basic unit of life.
  • R. Virchow (1855): Modified the theory by adding its most important corollary — "Omnis cellula-e cellula" (all cells arise from pre-existing cells) — explaining that cells are not spontaneously generated but divide to produce new cells.
Exceptions Worth Remembering
  • Viruses are acellular and non-living outside a host — they do not obey the Cell Theory since they lack their own cellular machinery.
  • Mycoplasma are the smallest known cells (about 0.3 μm), small enough to pass through bacteria-proof filters, and lack a definite cell wall.

All living organisms fall into two broad categories based on cellular organisation: prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Prokaryotic cells are the simplest and most ancient form of cellular life — they include Bacteria, Blue-Green Algae (Cyanobacteria), Mycoplasma, and PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms). They are generally smaller (1–10 μm) and structurally simpler than eukaryotic cells, and they lack a membrane-bound nucleus — their genetic material lies directly in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid — as well as other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, ER, and Golgi bodies.

Figure 1.2: Generalised structure of a prokaryotic cell (bacterium)

Cell Envelope

  • Glycocalyx: Outermost, sugary coat. A loose, undefined sheath = Slime Layer; a thick, tough, well-organised layer = Capsule. Protects against desiccation and host immune attack.
  • Cell Wall: Made of peptidoglycan (murein) — chains of sugars cross-linked by short peptides. Gives shape to the cell and prevents it from bursting or collapsing due to osmotic pressure changes.
  • Plasma Membrane: Selectively permeable structure lying just beneath the wall; controls entry and exit of substances.

Specialized Structures

  • Mesosomes: Vesicular/tubular infoldings of the plasma membrane that increase surface area; help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells, and in respiration.
  • Ribosomes: 70S type (made of 50S + 30S subunits), found freely in the cytoplasm. When several ribosomes attach to a single strand of mRNA, the chain is called a Polysome/Polyribosome, translating the message simultaneously.
  • Inclusion Bodies: Reserve, non-membrane-bound material — phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules, and gas vacuoles (in aquatic/blue-green algae, for buoyancy).
  • Motility: The flagellum (filament + hook + basal body) drives movement. Pili and fimbriae are hair-like appendages used only for attachment to surfaces or other cells, never for movement.
Common Bacterial Shapes

Coccus (spherical), Bacillus (rod-shaped), Vibrio (comma-shaped), and Spirillum (spiral) — the four basic shapes bacteria are classified into.

Fluid Mosaic Model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972)

The plasma membrane is not a rigid boundary — it behaves like a two-dimensional fluid, with lipid and protein molecules able to move sideways within the layer, much like icebergs floating and drifting in a sea of lipids. This is why the model is called "fluid" (molecules move) and "mosaic" (proteins are studded throughout, like tiles in a mosaic).

Figure 1.3: Fluid Mosaic Model — a phospholipid bilayer studded with integral and peripheral proteins
  • The membrane is built from a phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic (water-loving) heads face outward toward water on both sides, while hydrophobic (water-fearing) tails face inward, shielded from water.
  • In the human RBC membrane, proteins make up ~52% and lipids ~40% of the membrane mass — proteins are the functional workhorses (transporters, receptors, enzymes).
  • Integral Proteins: Partly or wholly buried within/spanning the membrane; many act as channels or carriers.
  • Peripheral Proteins: Loosely attached to the inner or outer surface; do not span the bilayer.
  • Transport across the membrane: Passive transport (diffusion/osmosis) moves substances down their concentration gradient with no energy cost, while Active transport moves substances against the gradient and requires ATP — e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which pumps 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ pumped in.

Cell Wall & Connections

Unlike the membrane, the cell wall is a rigid, non-living structure that lies outside the plasma membrane in plant cells, fungi, and algae — it gives mechanical support, shape, and protection, and prevents the cell from bursting when water enters by osmosis.

Figure 1.4: Middle lamella cementing two adjacent plant cell walls, connected by plasmodesmata
  • Algae: Wall made of cellulose, galactans, mannans, and often encrusted with calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
  • Plants: Wall made of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and structural proteins.
  • Middle Lamella: A shared layer made mainly of calcium and magnesium pectate that cements the walls of neighboring cells together.
  • Plasmodesmata: Cytoplasmic channels/bridges that pass through the wall, connecting the cytoplasm of adjacent plant cells and allowing molecules to move directly between them.

The endomembrane system refers to a group of membranous organelles that work together as a coordinated production line — manufacturing, packaging, modifying, and shipping proteins and lipids to their correct destination inside or outside the cell. It includes the Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER), Golgi Apparatus, Lysosomes, and Vacuoles. (Note: mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes are not considered part of this system since they don't originate from the ER-Golgi pathway.)

Figure 1.5: The secretory pathway — proteins move from RER → Golgi → vesicles → their final destination

Endoplasmic Reticulum

  • RER (Rough ER): Studded with ribosomes on its outer surface; the main site of protein synthesis and secretion — proteins are threaded into the ER lumen as they are made.
  • SER (Smooth ER): Devoid of ribosomes; the site of lipid and steroid hormone synthesis, and in liver cells, also involved in detoxification of drugs and poisons.

Golgi Apparatus

Discovered by Camillo Golgi, 1898

  • Made of flat, membrane-bound sacs called cisternae, stacked like a pile of plates, with a Cis face (forming/convex, facing the ER) that receives material and a Trans face (maturing/concave) that ships it out.
  • Acts as the cell's "packaging and dispatch office" — the primary site for synthesis of glycoproteins and glycolipids, and for sorting proteins to their correct address.

Lysosomes & Vacuoles

  • Lysosomes: Membrane-bound "suicide bags" rich in hydrolytic enzymes, active at acidic pH (~5.0); digest worn-out organelles, foreign material, and can dismantle their own cell (autolysis).
  • Vacuoles: Fluid-filled sacs bound by a single membrane called the Tonoplast, which pumps ions/solutes against their gradient. In mature plant cells, the central vacuole can occupy up to 90% of cell volume, maintaining turgor pressure.

Mitochondria and plastids are unique among organelles: each carries its own small circular double-stranded DNA, its own 70S ribosomes, and can divide independently of the cell, on its own schedule. This is why they are called semi-autonomous organelles — "semi" because although they can grow and divide by themselves, they still depend on the nucleus for many of the proteins they need. The Endosymbiotic Theory explains this: both organelles are thought to have originated from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell and became permanent residents.

Figure 1.6: Mitochondrion — cristae increase the surface area for respiration

Mitochondria

  • The "Powerhouse of the Cell" — site of aerobic respiration and ATP generation.
  • Double membrane-bound: a smooth outer membrane and a highly folded inner membrane forming finger-like infoldings called cristae, which increase surface area for the enzymes of respiration.
  • The fluid interior enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, containing mitochondrial DNA, ribosomes, and enzymes.
Figure 1.7: Chloroplast — grana stacks embedded in the stroma

Plastids

  • Chloroplasts: Site of photosynthesis; contain a fluid stroma and stacks of membranous sacs called thylakoids (a stack = granum), where chlorophyll captures light energy.
  • Chromoplasts: Contain carotenoid pigments, giving fruits and flowers red, orange, and yellow colours.
  • Leucoplasts: Colourless, storage plastids —
    • Amyloplasts: Store carbohydrates/starch.
    • Elaioplasts: Store oils and fats.
    • Aleuroplasts: Store proteins.

Ribosomes & Cytoskeleton

  • Eukaryotic Ribosomes: Larger 80S type (made of 60S + 40S subunits), first described by George Palade and hence also called Palade granules. Found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the RER.
  • Cytoskeleton: A dynamic internal scaffolding network of microtubules (thickest, made of tubulin), microfilaments (thinnest, made of actin), and intermediate filaments — together they give the cell its shape, mechanical strength, and enable organelle movement and cell motility.

Cilia, Flagella & Centrosomes

Cilia and flagella are hair-like projections from the cell surface built around a core of microtubules called the axoneme, covered by the plasma membrane. Cilia are short and numerous, beating in coordinated waves (e.g. lining the respiratory tract); flagella are longer and fewer, driving cells forward (e.g. sperm).

Figure 1.8: Axoneme (9+2) of cilia/flagella vs. Centriole (9+0) cross-sections
  • Cilia / Flagella Axoneme: 9 + 2 arrangement — 9 peripheral doublets of microtubules surrounding 2 central singlets, generating the beating/whip-like motion.
  • Centrosome & Centrioles: 9 + 0 arrangement — 9 peripheral triplets arranged around a central hub with spokes (like a cartwheel), with no central microtubule pair. The centrosome usually contains two centrioles lying at right angles (90°) to each other.
  • Function: Centrioles form the basal bodies from which cilia/flagella grow, and organize the spindle fibers that segregate chromosomes during cell division.

Nucleus Structure

The nucleus is the "control center" of the eukaryotic cell, discovered by Robert Brown, and houses nearly all the cell's genetic material.

Figure 1.9: Nucleus — double envelope with pores, nucleolus, and chromatin
  • Bound by a double envelope (two membranes), perforated by nuclear pores that regulate the two-way traffic of molecules (like RNA and proteins) between the nucleus and cytoplasm.
  • Nucleolus: A dense, non-membrane-bound body inside the nucleus; the active site for rRNA synthesis and ribosome subunit assembly.
  • Chromatin: The thread-like complex of DNA and histone proteins that fills the nucleus (term coined by W. Flemming); it condenses into visible chromosomes only when the cell is about to divide.

Chromosome Types (by centromere position)

Figure 1.10: Chromosome shapes based on where the centromere (red) sits along the chromosome (green)
  • Metacentric: Centromere exactly in the centre — produces two equal arms, giving a "V" shape at anaphase.
  • Sub-metacentric: Centromere slightly off-centre — one arm a little longer, giving an "L" shape.
  • Acrocentric: Centromere near one end — one very short arm and one long arm, giving a "J" shape.
  • Telocentric: Centromere right at the terminal tip — a single arm, giving an "I" shape.
  • Satellite Chromosome: A chromosome bearing a small segment attached beyond a non-staining secondary constriction.

Microbodies

Microbodies are small, single membrane-bound sacs found scattered in the cytoplasm of both plant and animal cells, containing various enzymes. Key examples include peroxisomes, which break down fatty acids and detoxify harmful substances by generating and then degrading hydrogen peroxide, and glyoxysomes (found in germinating fatty seeds), which convert stored fats into carbohydrates.

A quick side-by-side recap of prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic organisation, followed by the high-yield patterns most frequently tested.

Figure 1.11: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic cell organisation at a glance
Feature / OrganelleKey Pattern / CompositionFunction
Prokaryote Ribosome70S (50S + 30S)Protein synthesis (Polysomes)
Eukaryote Ribosome80S (60S + 40S)Protein synthesis (Palade granules)
Cilia / Flagella9 + 2 PatternMotility
Centriole9 + 0 Pattern (Cartwheel)Spindle formation / Basal body
MitochondriaDouble membrane, own DNA (70S)Aerobic respiration (ATP)
ChloroplastDouble membrane, grana + stromaPhotosynthesis
Middle LamellaCalcium & Magnesium PectateCell-cell adhesion
TonoplastSingle membrane of VacuoleActive transport in plants
Chapter 2 topics

Chapter 2: Overview of the Cell Cycle

The Cell Cycle is the precise sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesizes its organelles, and eventually divides into two daughter cells.

  • Cytoplasmic Growth: A continuous process throughout the cycle.
  • DNA Replication: Occurs strictly during one specific stage (S phase).
Duration Variations:
  • Human Cell in culture: ~24 hours
  • Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae): ~90 minutes
  • E. coli: ~20 minutes
Figure 1.1: Schematic representation of the Cell Cycle ring & phases

Detailed Breakdown of Interphase

Interphase is the biosynthetic preparatory phase where the cell prepares for division through ordered cell growth and DNA replication.

G1 Phase (Gap 1)

Post-mitotic phase. The cell is metabolically active and continuously grows without replicating DNA.

Genetics: 2n Chromosomes | 2C DNA

S Phase (Synthesis)

DNA replication takes place inside the nucleus. Centrioles duplicate in cytoplasm of animal cells.

Genetics: 2n Chromosomes | 4C DNA (Doubled!)

G2 Phase (Gap 2)

Synthesis of tubulin proteins required for spindle fibers. Mitochondria & chloroplasts duplicate.

Genetics: 2n Chromosomes | 4C DNA
G0 Phase (Quiescent Stage): Cells that do not divide further (e.g., mature neurons, heart cells) exit the G1 phase to enter G0. They remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless stimulated.
Figure 2.1: DNA content (C-value) rises from 2C to 4C across G1 → S → G2

Mitosis (Equational Division)

Mitosis occurs in somatic cells (2n → 2n), ensuring exact genetic identicalness in daughter cells.

Prophase (Longest Phase)

Figure 3.1: Prophase — chromatin condensing, centrosomes migrating to poles
  • Chromatin fibers condense into distinct compact chromosomes.
  • Centrosomes start moving toward opposite poles.
  • Nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi body, and ER completely break down by late prophase.

Metaphase (Morphology Phase)

Figure 3.2: Metaphase — spindle fibers attach to kinetochores; chromosomes align centrally
  • Disintegration of nuclear envelope is complete.
  • Chromosomes line up along the equatorial Metaphase Plate.
  • Spindle fibers attach to disc-shaped kinetochores on centromeres.
  • Best stage to study chromosome morphology & count!

Anaphase (Shortest Phase)

Figure 3.3: Anaphase — centromeres split; daughter chromosomes move poleward
  • Centromere splits simultaneously; sister chromatids separate into individual daughter chromosomes.
  • Chromosomes move to opposite poles (V, L, J, I shapes visible based on centromere position).

Telophase (Reversal of Prophase)

Figure 3.4: Telophase — two new nuclei form at opposite poles
  • Chromosomes reach poles and decondense into loose chromatin.
  • Nuclear envelope reforms around each chromosome cluster.
  • Nucleolus, Golgi apparatus, and ER reappear.

Cytokinesis Comparison

Figure 3.5: Animal cell furrow pinches inward vs. plant cell plate growing outward
Feature Animal Cell Cytokinesis Plant Cell Cytokinesis
Mechanism Cleavage furrow forms and pinches the membrane inward Cell plate forms in the middle and grows outward
Driven by Contractile ring of actin/myosin filaments Golgi-derived vesicles fusing along the phragmoplast
Limiting factor Flexible plasma membrane Rigid cell wall (requires new wall material)
Direction of division Outside-in (furrow constricts) Inside-out (plate expands)

Meiosis — Reductional & Equational Divisions

Meiosis is a two-stage process where a diploid cell (2n) undergoes two successive divisions to produce four haploid gametes (n). Meiosis I reduces chromosome number (reductional), while Meiosis II distributes sister chromatids (equational).

Feature Meiosis I (Reductional) Meiosis II (Equational)
Chromosome Number 2n → n (REDUCES by half) n → n (STAYS same)
What Separates Homologous chromosomes (one from each pair) Sister chromatids (like mitosis)
Centromere Behavior Centromere does NOT split Centromere SPLITS
Synapsis/Bivalents YES — homologs pair as tetrads NO — resembles standard mitosis
Crossing Over YES — in Prophase I (Pachytene) NO
DNA Replication Before YES — S phase precedes NO — directly after Meiosis I
Genetic Identity Two cells are NOT identical Four cells are genetically unique
End Product 2 secondary cells (haploid, 2C) 4 gametes (haploid, 1C)
Table 5.1: Detailed Comparison of Meiosis I vs. Meiosis II

Meiosis I — Reductional Division

Goal: Reduce chromosome number from 2n to n

Figure A: Meiosis I — Homologous Chromosomes Separate
Key Points:
  • Homologous pairs physically separate
  • Each daughter cell gets ONE chromosome from each pair
  • Centromeres remain intact (not split)
  • Sister chromatids stay connected
  • Produces 2 haploid secondary cells

Meiosis II — Equational Division

Goal: Separate sister chromatids (like mitosis)

Figure B: Meiosis II — Sister Chromatids Separate
Key Points:
  • Resembles mitosis exactly
  • Sister chromatids separate
  • Centromeres split during anaphase
  • No change in chromosome number (n → n)
  • Produces 4 haploid gametes
Figure C: Full Meiosis Journey — from Diploid to Haploid Gametes
Prophase I Sub-stages (LZPDD):
  1. Leptotene: Chromosomes condense as thin threads
  2. Zygotene: Synapsis — homologs pair, form bivalents
  3. Pachytene: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids
  4. Diplotene: Synaptonemal complex dissolves; chiasmata visible
  5. Diakinesis: Terminalization; chromosomes condense fully
Why Meiosis II is Equational:
  • No DNA replication before Meiosis II
  • Chromosome number stays at n
  • Only sister chromatids separate (like mitosis)
  • Produces genetically unique haploid cells
  • Result: Four 1n1c gametes from one 2n4c cell
Genetic Significance of Meiosis:
  • Crossing Over (Prophase I): Recombines parental alleles, creates new genetic combinations
  • Independent Assortment: Random orientation of homolog pairs at Metaphase I ensures each gamete is unique
  • 4 Haploid Products: Each sperm or egg carries one complete set (n) of chromosomes
  • Genetic Diversity: Without meiosis, offspring would be clones; meiosis enables sexual reproduction and species variation

Detailed Sub-Stages: Meiosis I vs Meiosis II

Side-by-side table comparison of every sub-stage across the two divisions of meiosis.

Prophase I vs Prophase II

Aspect Prophase I (Reductional) Prophase II (Equational)
Duration By far the longest phase of meiosis — in human oocytes it can be arrested for decades (dictyate stage) until ovulation. Brief and simple — no meaningful arrest, comparable to mitotic prophase.
Sub-stages Leptotene → Zygotene → Pachytene → Diplotene → Diakinesis (mnemonic: "LZPDD" / "Lazy Zebras Pace During Dinner"). No named sub-stages — chromosomes simply recondense and the spindle re-forms.
Synapsis / synaptonemal complex Homologs pair via the synaptonemal complex (lateral elements SYCP2/SYCP3 + transverse filament SYCP1), forming bivalents/tetrads in zygotene–pachytene. Absent — only n unpaired chromosomes are present, so there is nothing to synapse.
Crossing over Occurs in pachytene — recombination nodules catalyze double-strand breaks and repair between non-sister chromatids; resolved as visible chiasmata in diplotene, which slide toward the telomeres ("terminalization") by diakinesis. Does not occur — homologs are already in separate cells, so there is no partner to exchange DNA with.

Metaphase I vs Metaphase II

Aspect Metaphase I (Reductional) Metaphase II (Equational)
What aligns Bivalents (paired homologs, tetrads of 4 chromatids) align at the metaphase plate. Individual chromosomes (each still 2 sister chromatids) align at the plate — visually identical to mitotic metaphase.
Count at plate 2n total chromosomes, organized as n bivalents (humans: 23 bivalents = 46 chromosomes). n total chromosomes, individually (humans: 23).
Kinetochore attachment Mono-orientation — both sister kinetochores of one homolog attach to microtubules from the same pole (enforced by the monopolin-like complex), while the two homologs face opposite poles. Bi-orientation — sister kinetochores of each chromosome attach to microtubules from opposite poles, as in mitosis.
Random orientation Each bivalent orients independently (maternal/paternal homolog can face either pole) — independent assortment, giving 2n possible combinations (223 in humans). Chromosomes still orient randomly, but this creates no new diversity — the combination was already fixed at Anaphase I.

Anaphase I vs Anaphase II

Aspect Anaphase I (Reductional) Anaphase II (Equational)
What separates Homologous chromosomes separate — one from each pair moves to opposite poles. Sister chromatids separate — each moves to an opposite pole.
⭐ Centromere behaviour Centromeres do NOT split. Only arm cohesin is cleaved by separase; shugoshin-protected centromeric cohesin keeps sister chromatids joined, so they move to the pole as one unit. Centromeres DO split. Shugoshin is removed, exposing centromeric cohesin, which separase now cleaves — sister chromatids become independent chromosomes, exactly as in mitosis.
Movement / result Each pole receives n chromosomes, but each is still 2C (two chromatids joined). Each pole receives n chromosomes, now 1C each (single chromatid).
Genetic consequence Chromosome number is reduced here (2n → n) — this is the reductional division. DNA content is halved here (2C → 1C); chromosome number stays at n — equational division.

Telophase I vs Telophase II

Aspect Telophase I (Reductional) Telophase II (Equational)
Events Chromosomes reach the poles; nuclear envelopes may re-form around each haploid set; spindle disassembles; cleavage furrow (animal) or cell plate (plant) begins. Same physical events, but each chromosome is now single-chromatid (1C); nuclear envelopes re-form, spindle disassembles, cytokinesis proceeds.
Cell status after 2 daughter cells, each n chromosomes, 2C DNA — haploid in number, still diploid in DNA amount. 4 daughter cells total, each n chromosomes, 1C DNA — fully haploid in both number and DNA content.
Cell names Secondary spermatocyte (♂) / secondary oocyte (♀). Spermatid (♂) / ootid (♀) — these mature into gametes.
Next step Interkinesis — a brief rest period with no DNA replication, then proceeds directly to Meiosis II. Meiosis complete! Ready for fertilization during sexual reproduction.
Stage Meiosis I (Reductional) Meiosis II (Equational) Key Difference
Prophase 5 substages (LZPDD): synapsis, pairing, crossing over, chiasmata visible, terminalization Simple: chromosomes condense, spindle forms. NO synapsis, no pairing (n only) Only Meiosis I has synapsis & crossing over
Metaphase Bivalents (paired homologs, tetrads with 4 chromatids) align. 2n total organized as n bivalents. Mono-orientation. Individual chromosomes (each with 2 sister chromatids) align. n total. Bi-orientation. Meiosis I has pairs; Meiosis II has singles
Anaphase Homologous chromosomes separate. Centromere stays intact (shugoshin-protected). Sister chromatids remain joined Sister chromatids separate. Centromere splits. Individual chromatids become chromosomes ⭐ CRITICAL: Centromere stays vs. splits
Telophase 2 cells produced, each n, 2C. Secondary spermatocyte/oocyte. Brief rest (interkinesis — no S-phase) 4 cells produced, each n, 1C. Spermatids/ootids. Meiosis complete Meiosis I yields 2 cells; Meiosis II yields 4 total
Chromosome Count Starts 2n → Ends n Starts n → Ends n Only Meiosis I reduces number
DNA Content Starts 4C → Ends 2C Starts 2C → Ends 1C Both reduce DNA; MI reduces chromosomes
Genetic Diversity YES — crossing over + independent assortment NO new diversity — just distributes already-recombined DNA All variation created in Meiosis I
Type REDUCTIONAL (2n → n) EQUATIONAL (n → n) Defines the nature of each division
Table: Complete Sub-Stage Comparison of Meiosis I and Meiosis II

Key Insight: Why Both Divisions Matter

  • Meiosis I (Reductional): Splits homologs, reducing 2n → n. Sister chromatids stay joined. Where genetic diversity is created (crossing over + independent assortment). DNA: 4C → 2C
  • Meiosis II (Equational): Splits sister chromatids, keeping n → n. Like mitosis but starting with haploid cells. Distributes recombined chromosomes. DNA: 2C → 1C
  • Result: Without Meiosis I, you'd have too many chromosomes. Without Meiosis II, you'd have diploid gametes. Both are essential for sexual reproduction and genetic diversity.

Chapter 3: The Living World

The Earth contains millions of organisms differing in size, shape, habitat, nutrition and reproduction. This variety is called Biodiversity.

Characteristics of Living Organisms

1. Growth

  • Increase in size and mass.
  • Plants grow throughout life.
  • Animals grow up to a certain age.
  • Growth alone is not a defining property.

2. Reproduction

  • Asexual: One parent (Amoeba, Hydra).
  • Sexual: Two parents (Human, Mango).
  • Exceptions: Mule, Worker bees.

3. Metabolism

  • Sum of all chemical reactions.
  • Anabolism: Building reactions.
  • Catabolism: Breaking reactions.
  • Defining property of life.

4. Cellular Organisation

All living organisms are made of one or more cells.

5. Consciousness

Ability to respond to environmental stimuli.

Taxonomy

  • Identification
  • Nomenclature
  • Classification
  • Systematics — the broader field studying the diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships; it encompasses identification, nomenclature and classification.
Father of Taxonomy: Carolus Linnaeus
Figure 3.1: Taxonomy in practice — Systematics is the umbrella field built on the other three

Taxonomic Hierarchy

Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom

Figure 3.2: Taxonomic hierarchy — broadest category (Kingdom) at the top, narrowing to the most specific (Species)

Taxonomical Aids

  • Herbarium
  • Botanical Garden
  • Museum

  • Flora

  • Monograph

Chapter 4: Morphology of Flowering Plants

Angiosperms show incredible diversity in external form (morphology), yet every flowering plant shares the same basic body plan — a root system, a shoot system bearing stem and leaves, and (in the reproductive phase) inflorescences, flowers, fruits and seeds.

The Root

The primary root develops from the radicle and grows down into the soil. It fixes the plant and absorbs water and minerals.

Fig: Tap root, fibrous root and adventitious (prop) root systems

Tap Root System

  • Direct elongation of the radicle forms the primary root, which bears secondary and tertiary roots.
  • The primary root and its branches together form the tap root system.
  • e.g. Mustard, Mango, Pea (dicots).

Fibrous Root System

  • The primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a large number of roots.
  • These originate from the base of the stem and form the fibrous root system.
  • e.g. Wheat, Rice, Maize (monocots).

Adventitious Roots

  • Roots that arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle.
  • e.g. Banyan (hanging prop roots), Grass, Monstera.

Functions & Regions of the Root

Functions

  • Absorption of water and minerals.
  • Providing anchorage to the plant.
  • Storing reserve food material.
  • Synthesis of plant growth regulators.

Regions (apex → base)

  • Root cap — thimble-like structure at the apex; protects the tip.
  • Region of meristematic activity — small, thin-walled, densely-packed cells that divide repeatedly.
  • Region of elongation — cells enlarge rapidly, responsible for growth in length.
  • Region of maturation — cells differentiate; epidermal cells form root hairs that absorb water and minerals.
Fig: Regions of the root — maturation (root hairs), elongation, meristematic activity, root cap

Root Modifications

TypeModificationExample(s)
StorageTap root swells to store foodCarrot, Turnip
Adventitious root swells to store foodSweet potato
SupportProp roots — hang from branches to the ground for supportBanyan tree
Stilt roots — arise from lower stem nodes for extra supportSugarcane, Maize
BreathingRoots grow vertically upward for gas exchange (pneumatophores)Rhizophora (mangroves)

The Stem

  • Develops from the plumule; bears branches, leaves, flowers and fruits.
  • Bears nodes (where leaves arise) and internodes (region between two nodes).
  • Bears terminal and axillary buds.
  • Conducts water, minerals and photosynthates (transport function).
  • Performs storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation via its modifications.
CategoryModificationExample(s)
UndergroundStorage — TuberPotato
Storage — CormColocasia
Storage — RhizomeGinger, Turmeric
Storage — BulbOnion, Zaminkand
Sub-aerialRunner / Stolon (propagation)Grass, Strawberry
Offset (short internodes, rosette of leaves + tuft of roots)Pistia, Eichhornia
AerialTendrils (support, climbing)Gourds, Grapevine
Thorns (protection)Citrus, Bougainvillea
Phylloclade / fleshy photosynthetic stemOpuntia, Euphorbia
Fig: Common stem modifications — tuber, rhizome, bulb (underground) and thorn (aerial)
In banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum, lateral branches arise from the basal underground part of the main stem, grow horizontally, then curve upward to give leafy shoots (suckers).

The Leaf

The leaf is a lateral, flat structure borne on the stem, developing from the shoot apical meristem (SAM) in acropetal order. It grows at a node and bears a bud (which develops into a branch) in its axil. Leaves are the chief photosynthetic organs.

Parts of a Leaf

  • Leaf base — attaches leaf to stem; may bear two lateral stipules; expands into a sheath in monocots.
  • Petiole — holds the blade to light; long, flexible petioles let the blade flutter, cooling it and refreshing the air around it.
  • Lamina (leaf blade) — the green expanded part with veins & veinlets that provide rigidity and transport water/minerals.
  • In some legumes the leaf base becomes swollen — called the pulvinus.

Venation

  • Reticulate — veinlets form a network; typical of dicots (e.g. Peepal).
  • Parallel — veins run parallel to each other within the lamina; typical of monocots (e.g. grasses).

Leaf Types

  • Simple leaf — lamina entire, or if incised the incisions don't touch the midrib.
  • Compound leaf — incisions reach the midrib, breaking it into leaflets; the axillary bud is present only at the base of the petiole, not at the base of a leaflet.
Fig: Parts of a leaf — leaf base with stipules, petiole and lamina (with midrib & veins)
Fig: Reticulate venation (network of veinlets) vs Parallel venation (veins run parallel)

Compound Leaf Types

  • Pinnately compound — leaflets borne on a common axis, the rachis (midrib equivalent). e.g. Neem.
  • Palmately compound — leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole. e.g. Silk cotton.

Phyllotaxy (arrangement on stem)

  • Alternate — one leaf per node. e.g. China rose, Mustard, Sunflower.
  • Opposite — a pair of leaves at each node. e.g. Calotropis, Guava.
  • Whorled — more than two leaves at a node, forming a whorl. e.g. Alstonia.
Fig: Phyllotaxy — alternate (China rose), opposite (Calotropis) and whorled (Alstonia)

Modifications of Leaves

ModificationFunctionExample(s)
TendrilsClimbingPea
SpinesDefenseCactus
Fleshy scale leaves (bulb)Food storageOnion, Garlic
Insectivorous / pitcher leavesTrap insects to manage nitrogen deficiencyPitcher plant, Venus flytrap
Phyllode (flattened green petiole)Photosynthesis (leaf itself is small & short-lived)Australian acacia

Inflorescence

  • The shoot apical meristem changes into a floral meristem; internodes stop elongating and the axis becomes condensed.
  • The apex produces floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves.
  • The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is called the inflorescence.

Racemose

The main axis keeps growing; flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (oldest at the base, youngest near the tip).

Cymose

The main axis terminates in a flower, so growth is limited; flowers are borne in basipetal order (youngest at the base). e.g. Datura, Hibiscus.

Fig: Racemose vs cymose inflorescence — order in which flowers open

The Flower

  • The reproductive unit of an angiosperm, meant for sexual reproduction.
  • Four whorls are arranged on the swollen end of the pedicel, called the receptacle / thalamus.
  • Calyx (sepals) and Corolla (petals) are accessory organs; when calyx & corolla are not distinct, together they are called the perianth (e.g. Lily).
  • Androecium (stamens) and Gynoecium (carpels) are the reproductive organs.
  • A flower with both androecium & gynoecium is bisexual; one with only one of them is unisexual (staminate or pistillate).
Fig: The four whorls of a flower on the thalamus — calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium

Symmetry

  • Actinomorphic (radial) — divisible into two equal halves along any radial plane. e.g. Mustard, Datura, Chilli.
  • Zygomorphic (bilateral) — divisible into equal halves in only one plane. e.g. Pea, Bean, Gulmohar, Cassia.
  • Asymmetric — cannot be divided into equal halves in any plane. e.g. Canna.

Merosity & Bract

  • Trimerous (3 members/whorl), Tetramerous (4), Pentamerous (5).
  • Bract — a reduced leaf found at the base of the pedicel.

Position on Thalamus

  • Hypogynous — gynoecium highest, ovary superior. e.g. Mustard, China rose, Brinjal.
  • Perigynous — gynoecium central, other whorls on the rim; ovary half-inferior. e.g. Plum, Rose, Peach.
  • Epigynous — thalamus grows up and fuses with the ovary; ovary inferior. e.g. Guava, Cucumber, sunflower ray florets.
Fig: Actinomorphic (radial, divisible in any plane) vs Zygomorphic (bilateral, one plane) flowers

Calyx & Corolla

  • Calyx — outermost whorl, members called sepals; protects the flower in bud stage. Gamosepalous (fused) or Polysepalous (free).
  • Corolla — members called petals, often brightly coloured to attract pollinators. Gamopetalous (fused) or Polypetalous (free).

Aestivation

The arrangement of sepals/petals in a floral bud relative to the other members of the same whorl.

  • Valvate — margins just touch, no overlap. e.g. Calotropis.
  • Twisted — one margin overlaps the next, and so on. e.g. China rose, Cotton, Ladyfinger.
  • Imbricate — margins overlap but not in any particular direction. e.g. Cassia, Gulmohar.
  • Vexillary — the largest (standard) petal overlaps the two wing petals, which overlap the two smallest (keel) petals. e.g. Pea, Bean.
Fig: Aestivation patterns — valvate (Calotropis), twisted (China rose), imbricate (Gulmohar), vexillary (Pea)

Androecium (Stamens)

Consists of stamens, each with a stalk (filament) and an anther. The anther is bilobed and tetrasporangiate, with four pollen sacs producing pollen grains. A sterile stamen is called a staminode.

ConditionDescriptionExample
PolyandrousStamens remain freeRose, Lotus
EpipetalousStamens attached to the petalsBrinjal
EpiphyllousStamens attached to the perianthLily
MonoadelphousStamens united into one bundleChina rose
DiadelphousStamens united into two bundlesPea
PolyadelphousStamens united into more than two bundlesCitrus
TetradynamousTwo outer short + four inner long stamensMustard
DidynamousFour stamens in two pairs of unequal lengthSalvia

Gynoecium (Carpels)

  • The female reproductive part, made up of one or more carpels; each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), style (connects stigma to ovary) and ovary (enlarged basal part).
  • The ovary bears one or more ovules attached to a cushion-like placenta within a chamber called the locule.
  • Apocarpous — more than one free carpel (e.g. Lotus, Rose). Syncarpous — carpels fused together (e.g. Mustard, Tomato).
PlacentationDescriptionExample
MarginalPlacenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture; ovules in two rowsPea
AxilePlacenta axial, ovules attached to it in a multilocular ovaryChina rose, Tomato, Lemon
ParietalOvules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered by a false septumMustard, Argemone
Free centralOvules borne on a central axis; septa absentDianthus, Primrose
BasalPlacenta at the base of the ovary; single ovule attachedSunflower, Marigold
Fig: Structure of a stamen and a carpel; example of axile placentation (ovules on a central axis)

The Fruit

  • A characteristic feature of flowering plants — a mature/ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.
  • A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is called a parthenocarpic fruit (e.g. banana, pineapple, grapes — seedless varieties).
  • Consists of a wall (pericarp) and seeds. When thick and fleshy, the pericarp differentiates into outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
  • Mango and coconut are drupes — one-seeded fruits from monocarpellary superior ovaries. In mango the endocarp is stony hard; in coconut the mesocarp is fibrous.
Fig: Drupe (e.g. Mango) — pericarp differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp, enclosing the seed

The Seed

Ovules develop into seeds after fertilisation. A seed has a seed coat and an embryo, and the embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (monocots) or two (dicots) cotyledons.

Dicot Seed

  • Seed coat has two layers — outer testa, inner tegmen.
  • Hilum — scar where the seed was attached to the fruit; above it lies the micropyle (small pore).
  • Embryo has an embryonal axis and two fleshy cotyledons full of reserve food.
  • Radicle and plumule lie at the two ends of the embryonal axis.
  • In Castor, endosperm (from double fertilisation) stores food — endospermous; in bean, gram, pea it is absent at maturity — non-endospermous.

Monocot Seed

  • One large, shield-shaped cotyledon — the scutellum — with a short axis bearing plumule and radicle.
  • Plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths — coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.
  • Usually endospermic (bulky endosperm stores food); orchids are non-endospermic.
  • Endosperm's outer layer is a proteinous aleurone layer; seed coat is membranous, fused with the fruit wall.
  • Embryo is small, situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm.
Fig: Internal structure of a dicot seed (e.g. Bean) vs a monocot seed (e.g. Maize)

Floral Family Descriptions

1. Fabaceae (Papilionoideae)

Vegetative: root nodules; leaves alternate, pulvinate leaf base, stipulate.

Floral: Racemose; bisexual, zygomorphic; K(5) gamosepalous; C polypetalous, vexillary; A(9)+1 diadelphous; ovary superior, monocarpellary; fruit — legume; non-endospermic.

Br ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1

Economic importance: Pulses (gram, arhar, moong, soyabean); edible oil (soyabean, groundnut); dye (Indigofera); fibre (Sunhemp); fodder (Sesbania, Trifolium); ornamental (Lupin, sweet pea); medicine (Muliathi).

2. Solanaceae

Vegetative: herbaceous, solid/hollow hairy stem; leaves alternate, exstipulate, simple.

Floral: Solitary, axillary or cymose; bisexual, actinomorphic; K(5) persistent; C(5) gamopetalous, valvate; A5 epipetalous; bicarpellary, syncarpous, bilocular, swollen placenta, hypogynous; fruit — berry/capsule; endospermic seed.

⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2)

Economic importance: Food (tomato, brinjal, potato); spice (chilli); medicine (Belladonna, ashwagandha); fumigatory (tobacco); ornamental (Petunia).

3. Brassicaceae

Vegetative: herbaceous, solid, branched stem; leaves simple, alternate, hairy.

Floral: Racemose; ebracteate, bisexual, actinomorphic, tetramerous; K 2+2 polysepalous, imbricate; C4 polypetalous; A6 polyandrous, tetradynamous (2+4); bicarpellary, syncarpous, bilobed, parietal placentation; fruit — siliqua; non-endospermic.

Ebr. ⊕ ⚥ K2+2 C4 A2+4 G(2)

4. Malvaceae

Vegetative: axillary inflorescence, alternate leaves, bracteate.

Floral: Actinomorphic; epicalyx present (a whorl of bracteoles around the calyx); K(5) gamosepalous; C5 polypetalous, epipetalous; monoadelphous androecium (filaments fused into one bundle); axile placentation, hypogynous; fruit — capsule.

Br ⊕ ⚥ Epi(3-7) K(5) C5 A(∞) G(5)

Economic importance: Food (okra, durian); fibre (cotton, jute); beverage (kola nut); timber (Balsa); ornamental (Hibiscus); medicinal (marshmallow root).

5. Poaceae

Vegetative: fibrous/adventitious/stilt roots (maize); hollow stem, exstipulate; alternate leaves, parallel venation, sheathy leaf base.

Floral: Inflorescence spike/spikelet (male spikelet = tassel, female = cob/ear); bisexual (rice) or unisexual (maize); perianth reduced to 2 lodicules; polyandrous; trimerous; monocarpellary superior ovary, basal placentation.

% ⚥ P2 A3+3 G1

6. Asteraceae (Compositae)

Vegetative: alternate/opposite (Helianthus)/whorled (Eupatorium) leaves, petiolate, exstipulate.

Floral: Capitulum inflorescence made of two floret types.

Ray florets: bracteate, zygomorphic, unisexual, ligulate corolla, androecium absent, gynoecium inferior with basal placentation.

Disc florets: bracteate, actinomorphic, bisexual, tubular corolla, 5 epipetalous syngenesious stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous inferior ovary, basal placentation.
